opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is transparency and control. When you're doing research, or building on top of an agent system, you want to see what's actually happening inside the loop: how the context is assembled, how tools get called, how the model plans, where it fails. With a closed product, even an excellent one, you mostly see the outputs. You can't easily tell whether a failure came from the model's reasoning, the prompt scaffolding, the tool design, or the memory management. With an open architecture you can take those pieces apart and test each one.

For people like us who train models, that matters a lot. Agent capability isn't only in the weights. A big part of it lives in the harness: the environment, the feedback signals, how long-horizon tasks are broken down. If that layer is open, the whole community can iterate on it, compare approaches fairly, and feed what they learn back into training. You get a much faster cycle of discovering failure modes and fixing them.

There's also a practical side. Developers want to swap in different models, run things locally, adapt the agent to their own workflows, and keep their data under their own control. An open framework lets them do that. A closed one asks them to trust a decision they can't inspect.

I'm not saying closed products are bad. Claude Code is very polished, and a well-integrated product can give a better out-of-the-box experience. But in the long run, I believe the agent layer will look like an ecosystem rather than a single product. Openness is how you get more people experimenting, and that experimentation is where a lot of the real progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response values transparency, inspecting and testing an agent’s components, and adapting the framework, but does not clearly identify modifying its internal architecture as the reason.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Luo using OpenClaude to design a replacement for its multi-agent system.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Claude Opus 4.6 or claim that it was essentially the only model able to implement his desired modifications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer starts with what agents actually are now. A coding agent isn't a model anymore, it's a system: the model, the tool layer, the context management, the planning loop, the permission boundaries, the way it decides to read a file versus grep versus just guess. When all of that lives inside a closed product, you're not really using an agent, you're renting a behavior. And the behavior changes under you without telling you why.

What drew me to OpenClaude's approach is that the architecture itself is the thing you can inspect and reshape. If the agent is making a bad decision at the planning stage, I can see that stage. If the context compaction is throwing away the one constraint I care about, I can change how compaction works. With Claude Code, when something goes wrong, you end up doing a kind of folk psychology on the product. You tweak your prompt, you add a CLAUDE.md line, you hope. That's fine for a casual user, but for a team that's trying to build something serious on top of an agent, hoping is not an engineering practice.

The second reason is more about where I think the field is going. The intelligence in the model is increasingly commoditized, or at least convergent. The real differentiation is in orchestration: how you decompose a task, how you verify, how you recover from errors, how you use cheap models for cheap steps and expensive models only where they matter. Those are architectural questions, and they're the questions a company can actually own. If that layer is a black box controlled by a vendor, you've given away the part of the stack that's going to be most valuable to you.

And then there's the research side, which is close to my heart. We learn almost nothing from closed agents. We can benchmark them, we can poke at their outputs, but we can't learn what made them work. Open architecture lets the whole community iterate on the same primitives, and that compounding is how you get real progress rather than a series of product demos.

I want to be fair to Claude Code, though. The reason people love it is that the integration is tight and the defaults are very good. A black box can be a very well-designed box. My argument isn't that openness automatically wins today on polish. It's that for anyone whose work depends on understanding and controlling the agent's behavior, openness is the only thing that scales.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention Claude Opus 4.6 or claim that it was essentially the only model capable of implementing the desired modifications.

astra-6.text:
For me, the value is visibility and control. With a black-box agent, you can see the result, but it’s harder to understand why it took a particular path or where it went wrong. An open architecture lets you inspect those decisions, change how tools are used, and adapt the workflow to your needs.

That matters because an agent is more than the model underneath it. How you manage context, provide feedback, and recover from errors can make a big difference. I want to be able to experiment with those pieces and learn from failures. A polished product is useful, but an open architecture gives you room to build.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the value is visibility and control. When an agent does something unexpected, I want to understand how it made that decision—what context it used, which tools it called, and where things went wrong. With an open architecture, you can inspect those steps and change the parts that don’t fit your needs.

A black box can be convenient when it works well. But if you’re building on top of an agent, you need more than a good result in a demo. You need to debug it, evaluate changes, and adapt it to your own workflows. That ability to understand and improve the system is what makes openness valuable to me.
